segments.original: Although The Little Mermaid (1989), based on Hans Christian Andersen's story of the same name, was Disney's first fairy tale in thirty years, since the release of Sleeping Beauty (1959), and thus ushered in the Disney Renaissance, Beauty and the Beast (1991) is definitely the most important of the works inspired by these tales as old as time. This distinction might even be attributed simply to the fact that it was the first animated film to compete for the Oscar for Best Picture, but its qualities and differences are also unique, elevating a production determined to be, if not the best, the greatest of the fairy tales turned into films and of the other works led by female characters, including those under the Disney Princess banner.

When we compare the work's antagonist with the prince charming of the moment, we find an enormous discrepancy in how the animators present the two. Gaston's (Richard White) charm is an undeniable trait of the character, introduced as a true alpha male, although an extremely comic streak stems from this, all the more so because of the utter narcissism at the core of his being. On the other hand, when we are introduced to the Beast (Robby Benson), still in the film's opening, we come across a distorted, fur-covered, monstrous creature. The character design does not choose to make the Beast a being who, though bestial, is presentable; it dares to disfigure him as much as it can, lavishing care on his fur, unlike a certain live-action adaptation. As for Gaston's other traits, being the strongest of all or the hairiest of all, the antagonist ends up being no match for the Beast even in these attributes, the Beast being, initially, similar to Gaston in arrogance.

segments.original: On a final level, Beauty and the Beast invites the viewer to watch its character as a top-tier fairy tale turn into a strand inhabited by the most lavish, magical and grandiose musicals of all time, traits that also fit the work perfectly. First, regarding the ballroom sequence, Beauty and the Beast is part of Disney's investment in new technologies, such as those showcased in the visually impressive The Rescuers Down Under (1990). The ballroom, in this case, is made entirely on the computer, moving through the shots, something completely unprecedented for the company at the time, which was ambitious with this production. The daring camera movement lends value to the settings, allowing, as a result, an extremely fluid and enchanting flow, like a dance. Such grandeur is also noticeable in the exuberant colors of Be Our Guest. The musical sequences, therefore, had never been so lively before. With a very distinctive quality of animation, favoring the characters' movement over static presentation and seeking dynamism, the film finds formidable artistic value in many of its passages, such as the final fight between the Beast and Gaston, heightened by a rainstorm that complements the setting dazzlingly. Thus, the pinnacle of fairy tales is also one of the pinnacles of musicals.
